utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Before we resume, may I take this opportunity to rectify an oversight in the tendering of exhibits. The Court will recall that there were a number of references to the fact that the witness listened to quite a number of intercepted telephone conversations during his visit this time to The Hague, specifically, I think, on March 2nd. I had -- Mr. Robinson and I had agreed that the proofing note reflecting that list of intercepted conversations, and the witness's indication that he recognised his own voice and the voices of others in the conversation, would be tendered for admission. It's one of those circumstances where because of the agreement, that fell to the bottom of the list, and I simply didn't perfect that at the conclusion of the examination-in-chief, and I would like to do so at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 23099.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Shall we up-load it. Speaking for myself, I'm fine with the intercepts the witness recognised as his voice, but in other cases, he dealt with in his -- we didn't admit his statement dealing with those --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fairness, Your Honour, I wasn't -- I'm not tendering the underlying intercepts at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just that exhibit, the proofing note?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. And as I say, I spoke with Mr. Robinson about that, outlined the procedure. We also made sure that in any extraneous comments were eliminated and so this deals with those intercepts, specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no opposition from you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our position as regards the intercepts remains the same, so whatever the Trial Chamber decides.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are talking about this supplemental information sheet, proofing note, which you can see in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the accused's benefit, the agreement with Mr. Robinson was not understood as altering the Defence position on intercepts in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Prstojevic, do you like to say something in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would, and thank you for allowing me to speak. A few days ago, I listened to 27 intercepted telephone conversations, only one of which was in writing. Twenty-five, I did not wish to comment at all, though I confirmed that I did recognise my voice and the voice of some of my interlocutors. But I believe that I should not comment on that, but rather do it in the courtroom. Two of these conversations were eventually dropped as atomic bombs, because I had an argument with the Prosecutor -- or, rather, the investigator. And when he presented these two, one was in writing and not valuable at all. The discussion concerned old-age pensions, and I commented a bit on that. And another one which dealt with mobilisation. And I saw that the investigator simply did not understand that what was being done was legal and lawful and legitimate. He saw something else in that. And I am opposed to having conversations that I did not comment to be admitted as part of my evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. At this moment, what we admit is the fact that you recognise certain voices in these intercepts. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination. We'll give the number for that proofing note.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's Exhibit P2521.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see in e-court 65 ter 6591.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember, Mr. Prstojevic, that when we had the Joint Assembly session on the 25th of January, 1992, we had almost achieved an agreement, Cengic and myself, that the government should effect regionalisation and that we should hold a referendum? It was a well-known meeting next to the microphone where Mr. Cengic and myself were. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that after the break, it was unsuccessful again, and they continued to press their intention to slate a referendum?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the leadership of the SDA, headed by Mr. Izetbegovic, did not accept what Mr. Cengic had achieved with you and that it all fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Serbian version, it begins at the bottom, under number 21, so please have a look at the left-hand bottom corner of the Serbian version, where it says that the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted certain conclusions. But in the English version, I think we would need to move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: We should keep this page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian version, we would need the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will just re-tell this, so I wouldn't read everything. Anyone can read it. Point 1 talks about our position; namely, that the decision to slate a referendum was unlawful, that it was adopted against the positions of one of the constituent peoples, and that it can only oblige these other two peoples or that it would have to do with them expressing their will. Point 2: "Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina will continue its efforts to find the best solution for democratic transition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and best position for every of three nations on their common meetings. In case of reaching common solution, then the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina could accept referendum as democratic way for citizens and peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina to declare their will and reconfirm reached agreement." Mr. Prstojevic, was this Serbian position something that was widely known to the public in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including our officials on the ground?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it absolutely was well known to everyone, all the leaders and the people as well, because at the time the people very carefully followed what was going on in the Republican Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 1D3069 so that we can see how, a week before the referendum, you addressed the journalists and explained our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this statement from the press conference?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Point 1 says: "The Serbian people will not turn out for the scheduled referendum, nor will it participate in its work." That means that there wouldn't even be observers at the election posts; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Point 2 says: "The Serbian people and the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina will not present any obstacles to the Muslim people, or any other people, partaking in the referendum if they demonstrate an interest in it. We will respect the will of other peoples." And point 3, similar to point 4: "In its future work and political activity, the SDS will fully respect the will of the Serbian people and the leadership of the SDS of BH, in the interest of seeking a peaceful, durable and just solution for life, work and political activity in our Bosnian and Herzegovinian lands." Was this a sincere and fully applied position of the Serbian people and the local authorities on the ground?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was our sincerest position that we held on to as a matter of principle in the entire period preceding the war and even during the initial stages of the war. It was always our priority to try to achieve a peaceful resolution in any way that the leaderships would agree at the republican level. We always said that it was something that we would honour, and until such a time we strove to keep the peace and security of all citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that we had power in 37 out of 109 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly the number of municipalities in which we held power of the roughly 109 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I do know that in some municipalities, we had one. But I don't know the exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Serbian majority spreads over more than 60 per cent of the territory of BH?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, for the reason that the Serbs were sparsely -- populated sparsely the areas where they lived. Even in Sarajevo, it was the same. It was a larger area where the ethnic Serbian territories are. Then the areas where the Muslims are the majority, they are the majority only in the urban parts, and all the surrounding settlements of the city have the Serbian majority. That means they are not the absolute -- absolutely dominant ethnic group, but they are the majority in all the surrounding municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina we did not want to provide election lists, electoral rolls, or the infrastructure, or made any obstructions for the referendum?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. And in Ilidza, we did not obstruct this in any way, so this is 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please have 65 ter 1007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 18th of March, an agreement was definitely reached, the so-called Lisbon Agreement, the basis of which was the Carrington-Cutileiro Plan about transforming Bosnia into three ethnic republics?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that that was in mid-March and that an agreement had been reached, and it was a great relief for the whole people, for all the people in Ilidza and wherever else I was moving. But as we know, later on the Muslim leadership rejected this agreement. The Serbs would say they had changed their minds, when you accept it and then later on you say, Well, I cannot accept it any longer. And everything fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, we have a document from the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party, signed by Mr. Dukic, in which there is a request that the party be informed about the areas which can be included in the Serbian municipalities. Paragraph 2 says that: "The projection of the territory of the Serbian municipality should comprise the local communes and populated areas, or parts of populated areas, which will become part of the Serbian municipality." And the last sentence says: "... by Tuesday, the 17th of March, 1992, at the latest." Do you remember that at the time, all three sides were vying to declare, as fast as they could, what their ethnic entities would comprise?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, I don't remember this well and I don't remember this memo, but I know that, generally speaking, in Ilidza at this time, there was already a sort of tacit division, that the Croats had sort of their own municipality which covered the area of two local communes. We assessed that we had 13 or 11 local communes, and there were two that we shared with Muslims, and the Muslims at the time dominated in six local communes. However, as opposed to the Serbs and the Croats, they believed that they had the right to hold all of Ilidza. They were not satisfied with having just the local communes where they were the majority population, that is to say, where their population made up more than 90 per cent of the population. And I am generally aware of the Cutileiro Plan, and I have, to this day, the maps which were part of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that this did not have to mean a division with borders, but rather administrative division about who would be wielding power in the Serbian-populated areas, or the Croat, or the Muslim-populated ones?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was implied that certain territories would be ruled by specific authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that this request was made in the context of this conference and the expected date of the 18th of March, when everyone should have voted?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 65 ter 11698.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise these minutes and these people, and are these the minutes from the meeting of the Municipal Board of the SDS for Ilidza? Trnovo, but it was held in Ilidza; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just bear with me for a second. I have to read it, because I can't see it well. I do not see my own signature, and there are some other elements that I do not see. Yes, this is a document drawn up by the members of the Municipal Board of the SDS in Trnovo, because at the time there were requests made by the deputies and members of the Municipal Board of the SDS in Trnovo that the ethnic areas of Trnovo should be joined to the new Serbian municipality of Ilidza which was about to be formed. At the same moment, there were such requests by the deputies and members of the Municipal Board of the SDS from the Novi Grad municipality because of the 37.000 Serbs from the Novi Grad municipality. A new municipality, a small municipality, Rajlovac, would be formed comprising 3.000 people. At the same time, the representatives of the Kiseljak municipality, which bordered our municipality in the west, where there were around 800 Serbs, who were living right along our border and who requested that they should also join the Ilidza municipality. And there were also talks about the Hadzici municipality, but the president of the SDS from Hadzici, Mr. Ratko Radic, said that they wanted to be an independent municipality. And these activities of the legitimate representatives from these three neighbouring municipalities, and the Ilidza SDS representatives, headed by me in this period, were an expression, primarily, of a great anxiety and fear of the Serbs from this area about what would happen with them, because they were practically nowhere. I was personally in charge of these activities, I co-ordinated them, and we can see here that a certain division of duties or posts was already agreed and which positions people from Trnovo would have in the new Joint Assembly to be established on the 5th of April. And these activities, which can be seen from the minutes and which were ongoing at the time, had nothing to do with the Instruction 093 about setting up crisis staffs and so on. This was practically a self-organised activity at a local or, let me say, regional level, because the Serbian municipality of Ilidza will be formed. It was rather large, in terms of territory, but sparsely populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that according to our Constitution and laws, the local communes were authorised to request to belong to a different municipality, administratively; to be joined, in administrative terms, to another municipality if there were conditions for that? Was that part of the responsibilities of a local commune?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, and I think I'm competent to confirm that because since 1977, since when I have been living in the area of the Ilidza municipality and the Kasindol Local Commune, I was a member of the Council, and Assembly, and other organs of the Kasindol Local Commune. I was the last president of the Socialist Alliance of the working people in Kasindol. And I want to emphasise that I was a member of the League of Communists since I was a pupil in 1967, so I'm very well aware of the way in which the local communes operated. Since 1977, when I built my house in the Kasindol Local Commune, nothing happened there without my active involvement. The local communes had authority about deciding on street names. They were authorised to request reorganisation if that was in accordance with their interests; that is to say, achieving the rights of the working people and citizens, as the formulation was used at the time. So, therefore, I can answer in the positive and say that this request was practically in accordance with all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Mr. Izetbegovic withdrew his approval of the Lisbon Agreement on the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the date, but I do know that the Lisbon Agreement fell through because of the Muslim leadership, because it had changed its mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that you proclaimed the Serb municipality politically on the 3rd of January, I believe, 1992, and up until the end of March it wasn't actually constituted and did not start functioning?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. President, this is the way it was: On the 3rd of January, 1992, we established the Assembly of the Serb People of the Municipality of Ilidza. We elected the president of the Assembly and a secretary. I think that two or three decisions were reached, and that was it. After that, a press conference was held, and we didn't do anything more than that. So that was a formal declarative assembly of a preventive nature. The real one would be the one that would be established only later during the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 07177, and then page 21 in e-court. Unfortunately, this only exists in English, so I'm going to read it out, and the interpreter will interpret it. Page 21, please. Oh, that's it, yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read from that answer that you provided: [In English] "Look, political activity was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina aimed at finding a peaceful solution to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what our leadership was involved in. And the Ilidza leadership went along with that idea at all levels. At the local level, together with people from other parties, HDZ and SDA, we had talks in order to ensure peace in the area of Ilidza, and no matter what sort of agreement could be reached by our leaders, we would have accepted it. And throughout the war, the Croats and the Serbs stuck to that agreement, but due to an order of the staff commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think his name -- I did mention his name, but I think the order was dated the 14th of April, 1992, and the order was given to carry out an attack, and it was meant to be carried out by the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, that is to say, the Muslim forces, and they were ordered to attack Ilidza, and they did attack on the 22nd of April. We had 11 people killed and 56 were injured." [Interpretation] This is a page of your transcript in the proceedings against Mr. Krajisnik. Do you stand by what you said?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely correct. What was said here and what I said then was stated in several places. This is what I have to add: We always tried, number 1, to accept everything that was agreed upon at the top. Secondly, regardless of the security situation around Ilidza, in Sarajevo, when the war broke out, where people were losing their lives, we tried to maintain peace and security for the citizens. Had there not been external influences, regardless of the fanaticism of the Sandzaki from Sokolovic Kolonija, everything would have ended with just minor trouble. As a matter of fact, in some parts of Ilidza, the last local commune, Rakovica, in the north-western part, the local Muslims never attacked us. However, I saw many orders during the war. We were attacked by Muslims from Visoko, from other municipalities in Central Bosnia, and through the municipality of Kiseljak if the HVO would allow them to pass through that municipality. The order to attack Ilidza was issued by the commander of the Staff of the Territorial Defence of BiH, Hasan Efendic, I think that was his name, and it is dated the 14th of April. Our intelligence service found out, and the chief of the police station, Mr. Tomo Kovac, sometime around the 17th of April, informed me as well. And the vice-president, Nikola Koljevic, who sat in the Ilidza Hotel, informed us about this. And then at the session of the Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff was informed, the Crisis Staff of the Serb Municipality of Ilidza. And our commanders in the TO, who mostly held the rank of captain, reserve captain - there was also a reserve major - they knew that what was supposed to be set was only the day and time of the attack. I know, at the time, how disturbed we were by information coming in about attacks by the Berets, by the HOS, by various units that were technically equipped in this and in that way. This is what I'm trying to say: From the 3rd of April onwards, when the war started, I and the TO commanders did not sleep at home. We slept in Ilidza, the Command of the Territorial Defence, a new building that we took for ourselves, in a new building. We slept there. We were there day and night, vigilant, and we were waiting for that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have documents. We'll get to that. Could we please have the next page, 22, so that we finish dealing with this document. From line 7, I'm going to read it out: [In English] "And actually in the field, in many places, it had not been the case because Muslims basically, when we talked about the Ilidza area, and I've got proof of that because Muslims were better armed than we were, and they took over all the weapons of certain structures from the former Territorial Defence and special units of MUP at Krtelji." [Interpretation] Is it correct that the Muslim component in Ilidza had seized the weapons of the Territorial Defence and took the weapons, equipment and APCs from the MUP from Krtelji, where the special unit had been headquartered?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It is absolutely correct that the Green Berets and the Muslims, taking advantage of a certain agreement between the leadership of the MUP regarding division on the 1st of April, they took advantage of the situation. And on the 3rd of April, around 1.30, while I was having coffee with the president of the SDA and the president of the municipality, Mahmutovic, they entered the special base, Krtelji, that is, in the territory of the municipality of Ilidza, Donja Kotorac. Actually, it is in the middle part of Kotorac that is not populated. They took weapons without anybody's knowledge, because the Serb special forces, as far as I know, were so frightened that they didn't go to work on the 2nd. On the 3rd, when they hadn't arrived, this was a sign for the Green Berets to enter to get the APCs to Butmir and to Gornji Kotorac. We found out about that later. On the 3rd, I didn't know about this. And they took out everything that they could on that day. I found out about that only at twilight, you know, when darkness falls. You know when it gets dark. I received this information accidentally on the 3rd, and I immediately took measures. Between the 3rd and the 4th, there was even a conflict because of that special unit there. It is correct we have information from the political party called the SK Movement for Yugoslavia. The Muslims in that area at that moment were much better armed than we were. We did not have any combat equipment, except for small arms and anti-tank equipment. They would even get weapons from the TO from Pazaric, via Bjelasnica and Igman. They even got some tanks out into Sokolovic Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, is the transcript sufficient or should we have these two pages admitted as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these two pages could be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The less exhibits, the better we will be off. In that sense, I don't think it will be necessary to admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the transcript is sufficient, we don't really need to pile up documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, in principle, that sometimes the submission of a transcript -- a relevant transcript can obviate the need for longer questioning, and efficiently ends up resulting. In this particular case, I would only -- I don't have a particular objection. I leave it to the Court to assess the efficiency aspects, but I believe that that discussion continued into the next day. So if this is going to be submitted, we will be reviewing the transcript to see if there are further portions of the Krajisnik testimony relevant to this particular issue and to this discussion and whether it's only a truncated portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that may be a subject for your re-examination. I don't know. Let's please -- let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 1020.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Prstojevic, that the Muslim part and the Croat part of the Presidency, despite the disagreement of Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, declared general mobilisation on the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this very well, absolutely, because practically this was the beginning of the war. In a way, it was a declaration of war. The Presidency called that -- the people called that Presidency the rump Presidency because it had no Serb representatives. I remember that in detail. If necessary, I can describe all of it. I know all of that by heart. I know what Mr. Alija Izetbegovic ordered. This is practically a military matter, but that is where my knowledge seems to be the best.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the second part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a letter of our negotiating team, that is to say, Mr. Krajisnik and myself. This is addressed to Ambassador Cutileiro, and you can see now that we are telling him that we are facing a civil war, and that the situation is dramatic, and that they -- and that we were not sure that we would be able to continue contacts with him, and that Izetbegovic gave an order for mobilisation and a march to Bijeljina, a town torn by conflict. At the same time, strong-armed forces from Croatia are attacking Serb areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina and are killing people. Izetbegovic took some very irresponsible moves, mobilising the whole population. The state does not function, chaos is accelerating. This is also the way in which Mr. Izetbegovic is derogating the results of our talks. "Could you please help by exercising your influence ..." Do you remember that on the 26th of March, just before this, the 25th and 26th of March, there were entire columns of the National Guards Corps and other paramilitary formations that crossed the border near Bosanski Brod and committed a massacre, a well-known massacre, in Sijekovac?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina know this, regardless of the fact that information was being hidden from the media. But I didn't explain something else a moment ago. On the 4th of April [Realtime transcript read in error "May"], Mr. Izetbegovic declared general mobilisation of units of the Territorial Defence and Civilian Protection. Then, number 2, the reserve forces of the MUP. 3, weapons and military equipment were being taken out of JNA and MUP depots. It is quite clear that in this way, the JNA and the reserve force of the MUP were attacked, in a way, and that war was declared on the Serbian people and the Croatian people, because he's not the commander of the Croatian people, because the Croatian part of the Presidency, on the 8th - I remember that date - declared the establishment of the HVO army, the army of the Croatian people, of the Croatian community. Everyone knows about Sijekovac. It was the regular units of Croatia, I believe, that committed a terrible massacre of the civilian population, assisted by locals. But that's the way it is among the people. If that kind of thing happened, people did not expect it to happen in Sarajevo. They thought it was far away. But thunderstruck already on the 4th of April, especially in the urban area. That is why the 4th of April is called the Day of Blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are saying that from Croatia, it was the forces that were crossing the border, do you remember that the Croatian Army entered the area of Kupres, slaughtering all the Serbs that they could lay their hands on in the village of Malevo [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. President, I cannot remember the date. I think that General or Colonel Galic at the time was in this area. Then, later on, he would be assigned to be the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. And I know something about this from my conversations with him, but we had big problems where we were. We were following what the enemy was doing, and even though we had a TV at the TO Staff, we did not have enough time to watch TV. That was where we slept, worked, spent the nights, but I'm not really in a position to tell you any details about Kupres.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is a stamp confirming that it was received where it was sent. I think that's on the third page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D1189.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please have 65 ter 16771. I believe we also have a translation. I believe that 65 ter has a translation, so if we could please find it. I will read it, but I will also show another text which carries this as a new piece of news from "SRNA."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it says here: "Yesterday, on the 10th of April, 1992, a session of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly in Ilidza was held at which, among other issues, the general situation in the area of Ilidza municipality was discussed"? Can we please have 1D3053. It's the same, but formulated as a news report, and it has an English translation. 1D3053. Could we please have the English version as well. It says here: "At the latest session of the Ilidza Executive Board, held on the 10th of April, the general situation in Ilidza municipality was examined. Mr. Nedjeljko Prstojevic informed the municipal government that on the 5th of April this year, the Serbian Assembly founded and set up the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza with all organs of authority and administration. "Mr. Nedjeljko Prstojevic, the president of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza, pointed out that the peace and security in the area depended entirely on the Muslims and the Croats. The Serbs most certainly will not begin anything or disturb the peace in the area by any action. They will not do so even if, for instance, the last Serb were to move out of the Sokolovic Kolonija settlement, as long as this is done in a peaceful and civilised fashion. Thanking the Muslims and the Croats for their conduct so far, he proposed that the representatives of all three peoples should meet in order to preserve the current security in the area." Does this piece of news from the "SRNA" agency faithfully reproduce this statement for the public which we saw before this?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it mostly reproduces our statement faithfully, though there is an imprecision here at the beginning; that I informed the Executive Board. At the meeting held on the 5th of April, we had set up all the organs, and primarily the Executive Board; first, the Assembly organisations and then the Executive Board, that is to say, the government and all the others that were necessary, so that it was practically a joint session of the president of the municipality with the Executive Board. And it is completely clear that this was our position, the position we had before the war, during the war. And as for Ilidza, the war could have ended at any given moment, because our army would stop shooting at the moment when the Muslim army wasn't shooting. No one needed to reach any sort of agreement. The war would have ended by itself, because no one wanted to die, and we suffered the greatest number of victims in Republika Srpska. And what about municipalities that had 195.000 inhabitants, and we had only 25.000?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I then wrap it up, Mr. Prstojevic. You adopted a political declaration on setting up the Serbian municipality of Ilidza on the 3rd of January, but up until the 5th of April, it was not functioning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of April, the Muslims, the Green Berets and others attacked Krtelji or, rather, without any resistance, went in and devastated Krtelji, because they took away all the weapons and ammunition; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They entered without any resistance, and later on they would set fire to it. At the moment when we tried to oppose them, they set on fire the entire MUP special unit, and it will burn down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just help us now? When was the Crisis Staff formed, because it says here that this is the Information Service of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, we were doing this as we went along. My main responsibilities in this period were what I did by authority that I was given by the Assembly on the 5th of April. I was authorised by the Assembly to make decisions, issue instructions and orders, and do everything else as necessary that would be aimed at the defence and self-defence; that is to say, protecting the territory. And, formally, I would do it on behalf of the Crisis Staff, but the actual Municipal Crisis Staff was only formed by me on the 10th of April, at a meeting of the Municipal Board, when I believe I also set up our press centre. I could see that the previous document was signed by Ranko Mandic, who was chief of the press centre.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, could these be admitted, perhaps both of these as one number?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the numbers of the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm informed the documents are similar, and in terms of documents, they are virtually identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We cannot rely on that submission. So do you tender both the SDS announcement and "SRNA" news clipping, or is "SRNA" sufficient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have the translation, we have them both. We'll admit them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits D1190 and D1191 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have 65 ter 01502.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether what is announced here is that the commander of the Territorial Defence, Colonel-General Drago Vukosavljevic, was relieved of his post and that Hasan Efendic was elected to this position, with the task to drag Serbs into the war against the Serbs, as this document says?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's completely correct that Hasan Efendic was appointed to this position. And this is a statement from our Information Service which was already working, though people who were appointed to certain positions would be appointed on the 10th of April. But it was already active.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it the very same Hasan Efendic who, several days after his appointment, would issue the directive for an all-out attack against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did see this order in the war. An attack against the Yugoslav People's Army was practically ordered, an attack on the depots of the JNA and the MUP. And the third point was an order to attack, with the excuse of opening up the axis Ilidza-Hadzici, because Ilidza cuts through this area. And according to the sources that I'm familiar with, this was the first order for attack against certain ethnic -- that is to say, Serb-populated areas, regardless of what was happening in Bijeljina, in Sijekovac and Kupres. But in this case, there was an order by the commander from the very top, which means that the highest political leadership of the Muslims had to know about this. And this was the number-one person, that is to say, the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but just the Muslim part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 1D3070.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature in this document, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was your military logic from the other document, the A and B options, was that something that was accepted? You were the commander of the Crisis Staff at this moment?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. But when this Crisis Staff was set up, we forgot these instructions. It does not exist anymore, and I do not remember it and did not implement it. Rather, on the basis of the Assembly's decision and the newly-established Serbian municipality of Ilidza, I set up the Crisis Staff according to a certain organisational and establishment model. It comprised state structures and military structures, so practically the political elements were the fewest. And this was practically already in accordance with the strategy of All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection, and for that purpose, I brought it here. This is the strategy. It is the war book, and on the 22nd of April, the fifth column, it is known exactly who and from which house shot at it. It was a sniper. But that was the biggest document which regulated the combat of Territorial Defence units. And then there are documents to be implemented at lower levels, at the level of companies and detachments and the smallest units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who is under number 10? Obviously, they couldn't decipher it. Was it the chief of the Public Security Station, by his function?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, number 10 is the chief of the Public Security Station, Tomislav Kovac, and number 11 is the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff, Captain Obrad Popadic. After him is the chief of the Communications of the Territorial Defence, Vaso Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Jeremic, rather than Jeremija, which would be a first name. Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vaso Jeremic. After him is Rade Ristic, who was in charge of civil affairs from the eastern part, and then he is followed by Commander Novica Vulovic. He was the commander of the Territorial Detachment of Ilidza Centre. I cannot read who the last one is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Petko or Petar? One Petar, it seems?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, perhaps, one Petar Maksimovic, who was a commissioner for civilian affairs from the Blazuj Local Commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you set up the Crisis Staff six days -- or, rather, for six days while the combat and fighting was raging in down-town Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, because throughout Sarajevo there was terrible shooting going on. On the 4th of April, on the evening of the 4th, the Muslims used the combat equipment that they had seized from Krtelji. So from Butmir, they were firing at the centre of Ilidza, the headquarters of the SDS, the SDA and the HDZ in Mala Aleja. I was in that building myself in the evening when APCs were firing at that building and that area. From the 4th onwards, Ilidza was being targeted all the time. There was so much gun-fire that already in mid-April, they ran out of ammunition. We have information to that effect, we have proof of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 9387.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise this document? This is immediately after the Crisis Staff was established. Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a press release of our Crisis Staff, or, to be more specific, of the Press Centre, the Information Service. And it is signed by Nedeljko Zugic, a writer. He is providing information here on general mobilisation of the population, and he is calling upon the Serbs to report to JNA military units, to the units of the Serb MUP and the units of the Serb Territorial Defence. That is the only way for you to defend yourselves, your homes, your country and your families, from the assaults of Alija's army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After all, we can all see this. Let me ask you this, Mr. Prstojevic: According to our laws that were in force then, were these the only legitimate and legal military formations; that is to say, the JNA, the MUP and the Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. I would just like to add one thing here. Because we were under threat, and because mobilisation was declared by the Muslim leadership, I personally had to declare mobilisation immediately on the 6th. This is stepping up the mobilisation effort. It became even more topical at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that according to our law, the president of the municipality is at the same time president of the Council of Defence for that municipality and, practically, the supreme commander of the Territorial Defence in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was before the war too. The president of the municipality is the president of the Committee for All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection. The top officials of that municipality are members of that committee, as are officials of the National Defence and Territorial Defence. Practically, the president of the municipality is at the very top of the pyramid. He is the commander. Sometimes there is a reference to the president, sometimes there is a reference to the commander, but basically it is a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in accordance with that law, he has the authority to declare general mobilisation; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but this is what I was guided by here. On the basis of this strategy of DSZ and immediate threat of war, the Assembly said what they had to say, and then I, as an officer, went along the lines of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that at that moment, you did not have any other military formations except for the JNA, the MUP and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely correct. No one can prove that there was any paramilitary unit in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have specific information from three meaningful groups, who they were and what they were doing. I didn't agree with the Prosecutor on that the other day, so I would like to have that corrected. The man was diluted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it is only the legal formations that are being called upon here; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely the case. You can only use legal formations to defend yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D3071, can we have that now, please. It's not a very good copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this document. It seems that someone else signed it on your behalf. I'm not sure that this is your signature down here, but it is a document of the Serb municipality of Ilidza. Can you please tell us about this, especially paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day is the 10th of April. There were many meetings taking place. Many decisions were taken. A crisis staff was established. The head of the Press Centre was appointed, and, inter alia, this was released, this document. And it is my signature down here, although it is underneath the seal. Would you please focus your attention on page 2. I -- or, rather, paragraph 2. I clashed with one of the investigators on this. She said that it suited me to have a lack of order, anarchy, and things like that going on. I felt that that was really brazen. I found that it was work, order and discipline that suited me, and organisation too. I cannot read this either, I cannot read it, it's illegible, but I know all of that by heart. That's what should prevail in the work of the crisis staffs. I cannot read this further on, because we have a developed structure by now. In 20 or so local communes where we were, we were developing crisis staffs. And then paragraph 4, what is being forbidden is taking -- I cannot read this, but I know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Actions," that is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... actions without the approval of the crisis staffs and Territorial Defence ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "In particular"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... in particular, from fire-arms, except when this is done with the aim of protecting one's own lives." And I think that it also says "the lives of working people and citizens."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was one of the first orders -- this is the 10th of April, isn't it, or the 30th? It's the 10th?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 10th, and practically the OTP heard a series of my intercepted conversations where I say, Run, work, and then things will be fine. And that reflects my views as a railwaysman who worked in accordance with international rules regulating the functioning of railroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is only the necessary defence of life that is referred to here, right, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 08964.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you, Mr. Prstojevic, that on the 12th of April, we signed a cease-fire with Mr. Cutileiro -- well, cease-fire, cessation of all operations, and on the same day, the 12th of April, Hasan Efendic wrote that well-known directive, and the MUP probably sent it on the 14th along their own chain, then this attack that was carried out on 13th, does it seem to you like something that was not spontaneous at all, but rather implementation of Efendic's directive?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly the way it is. This is a lesser attack. But, strategically, the moves of the Muslim leadership of the Territorial Defence, or later the Army of BiH, are based on what the leaderships agree upon. You will see, on the 13th of May, exactly a month after this date, they will immediately, within a day or two, carry out awful attacks. Again, the same thing. Peace is agreed upon, but war is waged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3072. It's not exactly from hour to hour, but it is from day to day that we are following the situation through documents. 1D3072.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature down here? Actually, no, it says "For," F-o-r. Somebody signed on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Momcilo Ceklic, secretary of the Crisis Staff. I can recognise his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is? "Halting the activity of all --" It says up here: "In view of mobilisation, all activities shall be stopped."

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the text that I see here is practically illegible. I read one word out of three and then I realise what it is. In English, you can see it very nicely. Why don't you read it in English, please, so that I don't have to stutter and stammer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll try to do it in Serbian: "In view of the fact that general military mobilisation has been carried out, on the basis of a demonstrated need and the authority I have been given, and for security reasons, I hereby order: that in the territory of the municipality of Ilidza, the activity of all state --" Now I'm going to move on in English: [In English] "... the activity of all state, socially-owned, co-operative, private and other enterprises shall be suspended until further notice." "... other enterprises shall be suspended until further notice. "2. The activity of suburban public transport and --" [Interpretation] I don't see what kind of transport: [In English] " ... operating in the territory of Serbian municipality of Ilidza shall be suspended. "The following shall be exempt from this order: "A) food shops; "B) health-care institutions; "C)" something "of traffic." [Interpretation] I have "city transportation." Again, D is illegible. And E is: [In English] "Enterprises involved in supplying electricity. "All enterprises exempt from this order shall operate to a limited extent, and their activity will be regulated by supplementary instructions." [Interpretation] This was on the 14th. Was this based on the attack that took place on the 13th, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the attack on the 13th, but other attacks too. It went on all the time. Fire was opened all the time along the entire front-line, because the front-line was about 30 kilometres by then. The territorial units, practically the units of the reserve MUP, are facing each other.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we lower the Serbian version a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that subsequently -- no, no, no. Can we look at the top of the page, rather. Is this your signature up here, whereby you authorised this at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In English, it says "Trbovic?"

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it is my signature. I verified it later on. I was probably somewhere out in the field and the secretary signed on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break now, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can deal with another one or we can take a break, whatever you decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I ask for a small intervention? In the transcript, page 18, line 24, general mobilisation was declared on the 4th of April by Mr. Izetbegovic, and the transcript says "the 4th of May." Could we now please have 1D3073.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to have a look at this. There's your signature on the top of the page. Trnovo managed to link itself with Ilidza, as a larger and more powerful municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not comment on the document dated the 14th of April, where we halted the work of state institutions and so on. Let me just say this: That document practically verifies the situation that was already existing on the ground, because from the beginning of the war up until the 14th of April, the municipality was not operational. The security situation was such that many institutions were not operational, and we simply verified that. And the reasons for this were strictly security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that here, on the 16th of April, 10 days after the conflicts broke out in Sarajevo, itself, one Sarajevo municipality, that is to say, Trnovo, the president of the SDS and the president of the SDA, Radivoje Draskovic, and Alija Kucuk, made certain conclusions? And can you please tell us something about that. Please have a look at points 3, 4 and 5, where it says that efforts are being made to keep and maintain peace in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document and these conclusions, because Radivoje Draskovic was a member of our Crisis Staff, and the deputy president of the Trnovo-Ilidza Municipal Assembly was Mr. Nenad Lalovic from this municipality. This was an agreement practically concerning peace between the two major political parties. There was also a citizens' forum which was suspicious because it may include elements of paramilitary units, such as the Patriotic League. Do I need to read out what was concluded, because what was agreed and confirmed here was to maintain peace in the territory of the Trnovo municipality. It is one of the urban municipalities, but it is quite clear that the Muslims will not stand by this and that a horrible massacre would happen there, as well as persecution of the Serbian population. That was practically the worst massacre in the territory of the city of Sarajevo, and I mean the entire area of this municipality. They will be expelled, and those who didn't manage to flee will be killed, have their throats slit, massacred, and so on. And I even have -- I believe I have here some documents relating to this, where, in Presjenica, that was the neighbouring municipality next to Ilidza, in the month of July a massacre of 13 elderly people was committed. They were aged between 60 and 90. There was no combat. They were loyal citizens. They even had certificates to the effect that security was guaranteed to them. And then at a certain moment, they just cut their throats. And I believe I should have that somewhere here with me, the original minutes or documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, as I said to you yesterday, if you could keep your answers short and simple. Mr. Karadzic will take care of his questioning. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you the following: Is this proof that issues of peace, and preserving peace and good relations, were completely left to the local level, wherever this could be achieved?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. It was left up to the local level, even by the leadership of the municipality of Ilidza. In each of our local communes, there were authorised local boards. The presidents of local boards and commanders of TO staffs were authorised to maintain peace at the local level, and this was also the case with Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it thanks to that that in some places, there was fighting with the Croats, for example, and in some other places, there was no fighting, and does that illustrate the freedom of local initiative?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct, primarily thanks to local relations at the level of local communes and then also municipalities. In the territory of the Ilidza municipality and Kiseljak municipality, there was no fighting with the Croats at all throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 65 ter 07177. 07177. And in e-court, we would need page 159, and then we will move on to 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your testimony in the case -- I believe it's the Krajisnik case, and the date is the 16th of June, 2005. I'm going to read the question first: [In English] "Mr. Prstojevic, can you tell us about the visit following the starting of the uprising in Sarajevo by the Serbs during which you and the others [indiscernible] encouraged?" [Interpretation] And the reply is: [In English] "I've already said a few things about that: Namely, on the 17th of April, I think the Crisis Staff at Ilidza held a somewhat shorter meeting of the government of the Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was attended by Presidents Krajisnik and Karadzic. At any rate, the session itself was very encouraging for us, and I can only say one sentence that I remember very well that was uttered at that session. Dr. Karadzic said that no citizen of Ilidza should be harmed in any way, and to a certain extent, he criticised us. But our defence lines were not safe enough, and then they said, Yeah, you have these defence lines which are not safe and you want the government to be based to Ilidza." [Interpretation] Do you remember that the phrase which I used, and which is translated a bit differently here, is that no citizen of Ilidza, regardless of who he or she was, had to -- that all the citizens had to remain safe and sound?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was precisely stated like that. It's a well-known saying in the Serbian language. You have to take more than 100 per cent care that something should remain secure. Then you say, Not a hair on anyone's head would be touched. That is literally --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. Can we have this admitted, please? Or if I have read out everything, if it's sufficient to have it on the record, then it can remain as it is. I think I have read out everything that's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's the case. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have 65 ter 22231. 22231. In the English version, we need page 27, and in Serbian version, page 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 22231. It's a statement dated the 6th of May, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said -- it says it's a duplicate of something else, which seems to be a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that identification is [In English] document ID EN04-0243.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your interview with Mr. Stephen Margetts, and the last answer: [In English] "First of all, I never went to Pale without their invitation. There was a meeting in the Crisis Staff of the government. However, there was a meeting of the Government of the Serb People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, held in Ilidza, at which Karadzic, Krajisnik and Miodrag Simovic, the deputy president of the government, were present, and there it was discussed where the Government of Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina should have its seat. There were other representatives present at the meeting, but I, as a host, as a president of municipality where the meeting was organised, I was present there, and a few more Ilidza Serbs." [Interpretation] Is it correct that at this meeting, the main topic and the reason for our visit was to establish whether Ilidza was the place in which the government could be seated?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. President, as the president and as the host, in my introductory speech I talked about the situation in Ilidza. I glanced at my documents, and I noted the two key points: that we were trying to maintain peace by continuing negotiations with the SDA and the HDZ. And the other thing, if, God forbid, we would be attacked, that we should be able to defend ourselves. And the remainder was discussion about the seat of the government. And what is more, other people remember that better than me. A voting took place, because Minister Milivoj Nadezdin, who was from Ilidza, was an advocate of having Ilidza as the government seat. As far as I remember, the vote was four against four, and in the end, when that was the outcome, you and Mr. Krajisnik agreed on something between the two of you, and you said that people should go home and that they would be informed as to where the government seat would be located. And one of our men, who was the deputy commander of the TO - that was what he was at the time already - Dragan Markovic, he said that it was uncertain, if we were to be attacked by Muslims, whether we would be able to defend ourselves. And then you criticised us for that. You said, and I have said this many times, There, you want the government to be here and see what the situation is like and what sort of security you have here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I trust that what I have read out is sufficient for the record, we should not pile up documents. And if the Trial Chamber agrees, we can move on. Could we now please have P1489. P1489, that's General Mladic's diary. In both Serbian and English, we need the page 168.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is already the second half of 1995, and you still didn't forgive us for the fact that we did not come to Ilidza. We need the typed version in Serbian, and that's page 168. And in English, it's also page 168. We already have it in English. We can see that you said, and Mladic noted: "Our political leadership has been in chaos for a long time, and we've been betrayed several times during this war:" That was: "On the 17th of April, 1992, when they left for Pale; when the seat of government was designated; when the airport was handed over; when the army was withdrawn from Mount Igman; when some army operations were stopped and the eastern part of Sarajevo is not without a future." So you hadn't forgiven us this through to the end of the war, in fact?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that even today, the people down there believe that had the seat of government been located anywhere in the Serbian Sarajevo, the peace process would have taken a different course and matters would have been resolved differently. Secondly, as regards the hand-over of the airport, Vice-President Nikola Koljevic said that at that point in time, Ilidza was the most important municipality in Republika Srpska. However, as the airport was handed over, we found ourselves severed into three pieces, the western part of the municipality, the eastern part, and the Trnovo part. It was a very difficult situation for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that we were given the promise by UNPROFOR, and they undertook that they would see to it that we could use the runway connecting the western part of Ilidza and the eastern part, where the large hospital, Kasindol, was located, and that this promise was not honoured?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely true. However, we were in grave problems, and Mr. Koljevic, once he reached the agreement on the hand-over of the airport, nobody took care of the airport from that point on. It was mostly staff from the Muslim part of Sarajevo who were employed there, and for a long time after that we would be unable to use the runway at all. It was only at a time when UNPROFOR would assume these duties that we would be able to use the runway to transit the area, but that was a year later or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that because this promise was not honoured, our wounded had to travel four or five hours, rather than make a trip of fifteen minutes, and that we lost some of our fellows because they could not reach the hospital in time before the Zica Hospital was opened and even after that period?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, that is absolutely true. And I know soldiers, wounded people, by name from Hadzici and Ilidza who succumbed to their wounds as they were transported from Ilidza to Pale. What's more, some of my relatives were among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am sorry to hear that, but I do know that that's how the matters stood. But do you agree that this was not the only promise that was not honoured by UNPROFOR? Do you recall that we handed over an important feature, Stojicevac, to UNPROFOR, which had some very good residential facilities, which UNPROFOR, upon their departure, handed over to the Green Berets rather than to us?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that. But at that time -- my apologies. I do remember, but we regarded UNPROFOR as the European Economic Community. They were located in the Stojicevac and Serbia facilities. I have evidence to show in the form of protest letters that were sent to UNPROFOR, and I also have some correspondence with Colm Doyle, if that was his name, who -- they sided with the Muslims, and they were aware of the Muslim intentions to attack Ilidza on the 22nd of April. To put it simply: While we were constantly asking for permanent peace, they were asking for 24-hour truces. And on a crucial day, and I think it was the 15th of May, after a failed Muslim offensive, when the whole of Sarajevo was attacking Ilidza, both they and we had sustained grave losses. At that point, they would hand over the entire Stojicevac facility and complex to the Muslims. At that point, they would engage in a fierce attack on the 15th of May. They had enormous quantities of artillery ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we do have that point envisaged in our line of questioning, we'll go back to that later. Let's stick to chronology and let's finish with this document that we have before us. Mr. Prstojevic, does this not show that you were no one's blind follower, and even less a yes-man; rather, you were a person of your own mind?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Mr. President, my personal view had always been that where I was given an order from the top, I would check to see if it fit with the interests of Ilidza, in terms of security and economic interests. If it proved to be contrary to them, I would immediately oppose the idea and expound on it. In the event the person who issued this order stuck with his view, I would not implement the order if it went contrary to the local interests of the community and if it threatened them, and I was a local politician. The same sort of right was enjoyed by the people who held the positions in the local communes when it came to me passing down instructions to them. They were able to tell me that I was misinformed and that whatever I was telling them to do would go contrary to the interests of their communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prstojevic, is it not true that an enormous responsibility lay on your shoulders, and on the shoulders of those who headed the local communes, when it came to the possibility that the Green Berets would break through and massacre the population? Was this not the reason behind your persistence in fulfilling your goals?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you missed out on a very aspect of our defence effort. Our defence was successful precisely thanks to the lowest levels of the TO staff commanders, company commanders, platoon commanders, squad leaders. Even where the republican leadership or the municipality leadership did not live up to the expectations of others, they always did, because they had their own families, women and children, that they had to defend.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D1366, please. Can we zoom in and have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, is this your document, dated the 19th of April, 1992? Let me tell you, before you answer, that in some of the intercepts, they spoke of the fact that food supplies were not let through, and they raised this issue as a sort of justification behind their attacks. Can you tell us, what is this decision about?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was never true that we would not let cars pass through carrying food stuffs. Quite the contrary. We can have some Muslims who were eye-witnesses to the fact that I would be allowing them passage, in the interests of peace, even in the cases where they were clearly transporting weapons. For instance, a garbage truck for Sokolovic Kolonija and Butmir, a cattle fodder truck which it was quite clear who it was intended for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does item 4 not state that: "The following shall be exempted from this decision: Food stores; emergency aid; PTT enterprises; local food supply delivery vehicles; electric power enterprises; water control by the public utilities enterprise; SDK and --"

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Business banks, that's what it means, because the SDK was providing service for them: "The companies exempt under number 4 of this decision shall work limited hours from 900 to 1500 hours, with the exception of the emergency medical assistance, which shall work around the clock."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This decision was reviewed, as can be seen from the annotation at the top, also on the 21st of April, on the eve of the attack against us. It was our wish to be as flexible as possible. We didn't have any barricades on our intersections; we had check-points. People were passing through on their way to work in Sarajevo until the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Both the Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely. In our testimony, we always referred to the Muslims and Croats, because the Serbs are not considered as reliable a witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
