utterances.text: We can see here that even though there was a war on, voting was taking place, and out of the 10 of those in attendance, 9 voted in favour of maintaining the flexible measures regime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was this one person who abstained, and that individual believed that everything we were doing made no sense. He said there was a sea ahead of us and behind us, Ilidza would fall sooner or later. To put it simply, he was in favour of a surrender. We never held this against the man. That was his psychological make-up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3087.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a protocol from a meeting held on the 23rd of April, 1992, I believe, which I wrote -- or, rather, which I personally chaired -- or which I wrote, and it was chaired by the representatives of the EEC. Members were representatives of the SDA and SDS. This was after the failed aggressor's attack on the entire Serbian areas of Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the attack of the 22nd of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had 11 persons killed, 56 wounded. In certain books, they wrote -- they boast about the fact that they had only two individuals killed and that they were able to take over Ilidza, but that somebody had ordered them to retreat. You see, what was our undoing was our fifth column from within. They attacked us, and yet we sat at a table to negotiate with them. Their representatives were Avdo Hebib, I think, and Hodzic, Enver, aka Enko, because the official representative of the commander of the Crisis Staff, Mahmutovic, Husein, did not dare to show his face because he did not believe that things would end well. Nevertheless, we pulled it off. Some people came into a fight with Husein in front of the Serbija Hotel, and some people were killed, two brothers. We would be meeting with them on a daily basis from this day on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll be reading from English because it's more visible: [In English] "From the direction of Glavogodina, at 2120 hours, two rockets, one illumination round, and then the attack began on the Health Centre in Ilidza. "The firing stopped at 2400 hours. "For a time, we did not return fire, but then we had to." [Interpretation] Does this reflect what was happening as you were signing this document; namely, that you were being attacked from the direction of Glavogodina?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, this protocol was something that I was practically in charge of. What you are reading out now happened immediately after the protocol was signed; on the same day, but in the evening. This is my original handwriting, what I wrote there. I sort of jotted this down during the course of that evening. So this is authentically what happened at 2120 hours on that day and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A 120-millimetre and an 80-millimetre mortar is being referred to, and APCs?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, all of it, and Vehbija Karic, too, and asking the Croatian -- or municipality of Fojnica to help, because since their attack failed, they're trying to draw the Croats into the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the fifth column was your undoing. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, until the 22nd of April, all the Muslims were in the central part of Ilidza. As a matter of fact, I claim with full responsibility that more Serbs had fled, even those who held positions within the party, and others who held various positions in companies and so on, because they were afraid for their own lives. When the attack took place at the crack of dawn, then the Muslims, certain extremists, were shooting from snipers and hunting guns from the depth of the settlement, and it is well known from which particular points. The closest building to the Crisis Staff and to the TO on the front-line was Fijaker. From there, it is well known who lived there, so it was from there that the TO staff was fired at. Two soldiers were wounded in front. The man was lying and hit in the leg. Another person was hit by a bullet in the buttocks. I ran out of the staff and asked what was going on, where was the gun-fire coming from, because there were people who were older than I am now who were guarding the staff building. I practically opened fire at that other building, and I prepared a group for a search to find the sniper there. The man who was there, it was sufficient for him to run 50 metres and no one would touch him afterwards. He could just get lost in the crowd. This attack was filmed by 10 TV cameras before the eyes of the European Economic Community; inter alia, TV Sarajevo, the official Muslim TV, allowed the filming of this -- was allowed to film this. And from there, you can see our people who got killed. You can see that from the institute. That's the Institute for Rehabilitation. It's a health institution. You can see the dead. You can see when a sniper hits a cameraman - I think it was a BBC cameraman - in the right hand. And, unfortunately, some Robert Donia, in General Milosevic's materials, claimed that we were the ones who were shelling that institute and that we opened sniper fire at it, and that was within our territory. I am mentioning this as an example of the kind of bad mistake that an expert can make and thereby create the wrong picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I be allowed to summarise what you were saying? You are attacked by the Green Berets and the Muslim Territorial Defence from the territory that is not under your control, and you were fired at -- or you were shot in the back by Muslims who lived in Serb-held territory. Does that correspond to what you were trying to say? And this gun-fire came from Fijaker, that was under Serb control, and the institute that was under Serb control; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now have 65 ter 30689.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 20th of April, this is a telephone conversation between Cedo Kljajic and Tomislav Kovac. Is it true that Tomislav Kovac is the local police chief and Cedo Kljajic is some official in the Ministry of the Police or, rather, of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Mr. Kovac was the chief of the police station in Ilidza, and Cedo is a high official at the Security Centre of Serbian Sarajevo in Vraca.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they were in the police before that as well, that they are not any kind of new policemen?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is fully correct. They are professionals in the MUP; that is to say, starting with school and then the prewar period. As a matter of fact, Mr. Kovac was for a long time a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia before the war, and so was I ever since I was a pupil. And, as a matter of fact, Mr. Kovac was not even a member of the SDS at that point in time, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at this part, where it says: "All top officials of the MUP ," that's what Kljajic says. And then he says that they went to Presidency with a single request; that they be allowed to break through all barricades on the approaches to the city of Sarajevo? And then Kovac says: "Yes." And Cedo Kljajic says now they are counting on that solution, and they are going to try that during the afternoon and night hours. So Cedo is saying that the Muslim part of the police is asking for permission for an armed breakthrough, and Kljajic says: "All of those conversations that we had previously are no longer valid." And down here, he says: "See, they are consolidating their forces. They are going to try a break through, and we don't know which way, and it is most probable that they will first try to do this through Ilidza." And then towards the bottom in Serbian: "Well, I cannot reach Prstojevic. I did not even talk to him, so if you talk to him, convey this message to him." Does this correspond to the situation as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in this period I heard about this day when several conversations took place. It was believed that we, the Territorial Defence, headed by yours truly, imposed strict controls that were not justified. However, after these conversations - there is one of Cedo's, one of Mr. Mandic's - Cedo learned something else, but he's making a mistake. It's not that the Muslim leaders of the MUP went there because they wanted to do so themselves. They were asked by the Muslim leadership, and they were asked to carry out an order of the 14th of April. We have information - I even have it here - to the effect that at that moment, about 3.600 members of the Green Berets, the Patriotic League, the Muslim TO and the HOS were about to attack us. He sees that we are about to be attacked. Attacks were announced to us every day through different channels, but we knew about this. On the 21st, I tried to prevent an attack. I shall talk to MP Ljubo Bosiljcic in Sokolovic Kolonija, then the president of the Association of World War II Veterans, Sveto Dragovic, and a member of the League of Communists Movement for Yugoslavia, Milenko Jaslar. However, as for these talks in Sokolovic Kolonija around 2100 hours, Juka Prazina, one of the commanders of the paramilitaries and later on a general in the police of the MUP, he will shew them away because they stood in his way, in the way of the attack that would follow in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, or, rather, marked for identification for well-known reasons in view of the position we hold?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to that issue later on. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have 65 ter 30709.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a day later, the 21st of April, 1992. This is a conversation between yourself and Momo Garic. On page 1, we see that he is asking to speak to you, and he's calling from Novo Sarajevo, New Sarajevo. The next page, please, in English and in Serbian. Garic is providing information to you here - it's line 4 and 5 from the top - that the army cannot do anything about the tanks: "We are encircled. Do you have any armour, manpower? Please, I'm begging you." And then this man is handing over the receiver to you because you were just coming in. Garic is complaining that they were encircled and that the army did not want to get involved. Can we have page 3. And then you are asking: "Where are you?" And then he is trying to mollify someone and saying: "In Vraca." And then: "Where in Vraca? Are you by the MUP down there or up there? Someone will be waiting for those people there by the underpass." Can we have the next page in Serbian and in English. He's asking you for help: "We went down to a town by Miljacka. They're too strong. They are encircling us, and the army refuses to move." And then you say: "Wait a second. Are you fighting there?" And Garic says: "We are fighting fiercely. We have many casualties, dead and wounded." And then further down, you say: "What are the special forces doing?" And he says: "They don't want to leave the compound. There you go." And: "The reserve police force also made a promise." Can we have page 6 in English and the next page in Serbian. Your question is: "Where is the fighting actually taking place?" And he's saying: "Vrbanja, Grbavica, Ivan Krndelj, all the way to Elektroprivreda." We see all of it. And then, tell us, is it true that Grbavica, like all of New Sarajevo, after all, is a predominantly Serb-populated area and that the Muslim Green Berets and paramilitaries are attacking Grbavica on that day, on the 21st of April, and Momo Garic is asking that you send in some help?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is quite correct. That is in line with the tactics of the Muslim Territorial Defence, because they are attacking on several fronts. According to some documents, in 1995, in the territory of Novo Sarajevo, there is a negligible difference between Serbs and Muslims, in terms of the census. And Grbavica, with its surrounding area -- I mean, people said that Grbavica was a dormitory. It was a newly-built area. The population was predominantly Serb, and lots of JNA officers had their apartments there and so on and so forth. As for Mr. Garic and his men, I spoke to them several times during that day. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence there. I did not really know the man very well until then, and I'm giving him advice here, because I see that the JNA doesn't want to do anything. They didn't take part in anything on the 22nd of April either. They didn't help us at all, us in Ilidza. They were rather reserved. Also, here they hardly did anything. Those who fought the best were ordinary soldiers who were defending their own homes. I was in a difficult situation here, but, nevertheless, I did prepare a unit for him, a platoon from Kasindol, taking the shortest route possible in order to help. And you see already the next day, there would be an attack against us over here. It is quite clear that the attacks were synchronised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that a soldier who defend his home, et cetera. Is there anyone here, except for the local population, that actually lives there? I mean, among these Serb forces of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. In Ilidza, absolutely no one else. And from this conversation, you see there's no one else. The only reference is to the entire local population being mobilised. The MUP is trying to avoid a fight, and it is well known that the JNA didn't want to fight in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think -- we don't need to mark it for identification, since Mr. Prstojevic acknowledged it's his voice. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 65 ter 1036.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, if you can familiarise yourself with this document. It was issued and signed by me. It says here that on the 22nd of April, 1992, in the early morning hours -- and can you describe to us, just briefly, what this document says?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here you give an announcement that in the early morning hours on the 22nd of April, an attack was launched on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza by the Sokolovic Kolonija. But, President, this was an attack from the entire 16-kilometre line along which we bordered the Muslim ethnic space. Then further on you say that there is a large number of wounded and dead, and you appeal to all individuals and commanders to stop the conflict unconditionally. You emphasise that the fighting and the attacks on Grbavica, as well as on Ilidza, as we have seen, were aimed at obstructing the peace process and the coming of Lord Carrington, and thus make it impossible to have a peaceful resolution of the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 65 ter 08175. 08175. And in the English version in e-court, we would need page 76, and in the Serbian version, 86.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your statement from 2003. I shall read it in English because I have it in English. And you can control, in Serbian, whether the translation is good: [In English] "On 22nd of April, besides all the agreements about cease-fire, unannounced, without announcement, the Muslim forces attacked Ilidza at 5.00 and 45 minutes in the morning, and they attacked regular police, reserve police and Territorial Defence. We had 11 dead and 56 wounded. So how that happened and who was attacking who was recorded by at least 20 cameras of journalists that were located in Hotel Srbija at that time. And there is an authentic movie of the BBC cameraman. And I know that person who lives in Ilidza and he still has that movie and he can give it to you. According to the information that we have today, only two Muslim soldiers got killed, out of which one was Albanian, that means foreigner," Albanian from Albania, probably, "and I have a book here in my bag where the Muslim commander writes about that attack on Ilidza. That is a very good -- another document that speaks about who was who." [Interpretation] Does this correspond with what you said, and does it correspond with what took place?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely correct. But let me also add something on the number of cameras. As you can see, I now said 10. It always seems that the number is smaller than it is. A number of people, cameramen, had made certain recordings which are now on the Internet, and certain clips about this fighting can be found. It has been recorded from a number of angles.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is what I read out sufficient or should we have it admitted? From the point of view of the Defence, I think this is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have in e-court P1489. That is General Mladic's diary, P1489, and the page in both Serbian and English that we need is 167. But in the Serbian version, if we could please have the type-scripted page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, you were with General Mladic. There's one "Gogovac," but probably "Glogovac." And it says then, President Prstojevic: "Ilidza municipality makes up one-third of Serbian Sarajevo. "We had 3.001 wounded and 930 dead and 150 civilian victims of war." Mr. Prstojevic, is this a frightening result, considering such a small area?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the result is frightening. Miso Glogovac, who is mentioned was the director of the construction company Put, or The Road. However, here with me I have the most correct data which I prepared during the winter. The exact number is 3.001 soldiers who were wounded. Practically, every second fighter in Ilidza was wounded, and every eighth died. The number of -- of the soldiers who died, of the 861, because here they were mixed with the civilians, but the number was higher, the number was the highest in Republika Srpska, and Banja Luka has 195.000 inhabitants. And the other number, 3.001 -- or I am wrong. The number of wounded is the highest and the number of the dead is the second highest. As for the civilian casualties, from what I established, in the territory that the Ilidza municipality controlled, the number was around 210. That included the Serbs, the Muslims and the Croats, because we did not divide civilian casualties on the basis of ethnicity. However, due to the set of circumstances in the Muslim part of Ilidza, in Dobrinja, and in the Croatian-populated part which, over time, the Muslims will take over by force, it was 208, what I managed to establish in winter. That's the number of the Serbs who lost their lives. They were mostly taken away from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it a fact that you had many refugees, and that you were literally living on the confrontation line or the separation line, that you were within reach of all sorts of weapons, and that this was decisive both for the number of casualties and also the state of mind, I mean, the fear that the population was living in, and also the sort of responsibility that you were feeling, as the leadership in the area?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first refugees in Ilidza practically arrived from the parts of Ilidza which were under Muslim control, and these were Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica. And as early as by the 28th of April or so, all the Serbian population fled as refugees from these two local communes, whoever could. Around 100 Serbs remained in Sokolovic Kolonija, and around 300 remained in Hrasnica. At that moment, we already had around 4.000 refugees in the centre of Ilidza. They were accommodated with their relatives and in a car camping site in Ilidza, and also at the Forestry School, some of them, and that school was later on transformed into barracks. Another important thing is that refugees from down-town Sarajevo were arriving daily. Refugees from Central Bosnia were also beginning to arrive through Kiseljak. And in this period, more than 30.000 Serbs left Central Bosnia via Kiseljak. There are reports about that, some of them very touching, because people sometimes left barefoot or in their socks. I have two reports. One is from the commander of the Igman Brigade and another one from the president of the Local Commune Rakovica, which was the first one to receive these refugees. And to cut the long story short, the population of Ilidza, which we were controlling, I mean, in that part of Ilidza, grew from 20-odd thousand during this period, according to some estimates, to almost 40.000, and there were fluctuations all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct, Mr. Prstojevic, that with such a high number of refugees and the doubling of the population, and also considering the fact that some of the local Muslims were shooting at them from behind their backs, was it difficult to maintain public order in the Serbian-populated part of Ilidza? Was it difficult to come to terms with the population, who were impoverished and afraid and so on? Was it difficult for you, as the president of the municipality, to deal with all this?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in the early stages, before the Army of Republika Srpska was established and throughout 1992, the situation was very difficult. What is more, there is a document issued by the chief of the -- Colonel Marcetic from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, who said at the end - I think he wrote that in December - that no one's life could be guaranteed in this region, because a group arrested even him at the hotel in Vogosca, where he was sleeping. There was great disturbance and unrest, even though the local citizens, the Serbs, were very tolerant and very mild. But if someone lost two brothers or two sisters, there were whole families in Sarajevo that perished. Such people acted in a manner that was uncontrollable. And I will emphasise: In this period, Ilidza municipality was fired on once, and I had to move everyone out of the municipality, except for myself, I remained there. And it was only by chance that the municipality building was not set on fire, because the Zolja shell hit a tree rather than a specific office. It also happened that Serbs would kill one another. The League of Communists Movement for Yugoslavia was also very strong, and it co-operated with its elements across Sarajevo. So as civilian authorities, we hardly managed to maintain our positions. And when the Muslims and their units did not kill me, it almost happened that Serbs killed me. It was really very critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thanks a lot. Now I will try to ask you to identify certain documents, mostly originating from you. And if possible, I would ask you for as short answers as possible, because otherwise we cannot do everything that we envisaged. When you said that someone fired at the municipality, you actually meant the municipality building, the seat of the municipal authorities, and that you had to evacuate the building; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it happened twice, and the Serbs fired at me; once, before September, and the next time it was on the 1st of September. And the Muslims were targeting the municipality building all along. In October 1992, a shell killed eight passengers and wounded 33 passengers at a bus stop in front of the municipality building, and the shell was fired from the Muslim part. And the eight casualties included, for example, two sisters who were Croats by ethnicity. I knew them. And at the moment I ran out of the municipality building to try to save them, when they fell down, because it was a real disaster --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please have 1D1369. I will now try to move as quickly as possible through these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your document, so I hope you will be able to confirm what it is, and the others will be able to read what it refers to. Is this your document, dated the 26th of April? The English version is contained on a single page, so I would ask the parties to pay attention to it. Can we now just say briefly whether this your documents and what it deals with? But as briefly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's our document, but I cannot see a signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your signature is on the second page? In the Serbian version, it's the second page?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is a memo sent to the representative of UNPROFOR -- or, rather, the European Economic Community, in which, as far as I can say, on the top of my head, I have no time to read.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please bring back the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You talk about the attack on the 22nd, and then you also say that: "We have reliable information that one of the vehicles transported Avdo Hebib, the special adviser in the MUP." I believe that somewhere you mention the possibility that they might be painting their vehicles white. Could we now please have a look at the second page.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that you used your combat vehicles to shield the Muslims from Hrasnica. And then further on: "The Green Berets paint their vehicles white to camouflage them ..." And so on and so forth. Is this an authentic letter which you sent?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we protest, because they engaged in fighting and they drove around Muslim officials who were recording our combat lines. We also had reliable information that on the 21st of April, they had a meeting with the SDA at the Stojicevac Hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3054, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your letter to Ferrera and Mr. Doyle, dated the 30th of April, 1992. And you say that at 9.55 of the 29th of April, 1992, the Green Berets opened heavy fire from the direction of Sokolovic Kolonija at the Forestry School, et cetera, et cetera: "We returned fire 20 minutes later, when our soldiers started getting wounded." Can you confirm that the events and the letter are authentic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that this is my signature and that the document is authentic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please admit the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3074, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a public announcement of the Crisis Staff, dated the 1st of May, 1992, where you inform the public of the disinformation coming from some media that the Serbian authorities of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza have blocked Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica and Butmir settlements: "We emphasise once again that access has been made possible for vehicles transporting food stuffs, and particularly milk and bread, in the whole territory of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, including Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir and Hrasnica." You go on to say: "We would like to emphasise that the Serbian authorities of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza allow freedom of movement across the territory of the municipality to all people, regardless of their ethnicity, party affiliation, sex, or any other affiliation." Is this true, and did you issue this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is our document, and this is true. And that was the way we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D1206.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D01276, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, when a Serb or a Muslim wanted to cross the lines or approach our lines, would he have asked the authorities to issue him with a certificate of some sort testifying to his involvement in a work detail, proving that he was not a deserter?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. But I believe that by this time, you already had certain forms granting permission to leave. Primarily, this was meant for our military conscripts, the Serbs. But until the 14th of May, whoever knew which route to take could move about, but there were certain permissions of this sort being issued in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this letter, you write to Ferrera and Doyle. The translation reads "Sereda," and I believe it's "Ferrera" in Serbian. Do you recall the document, although it's a very poor copy, but at the bottom it says that in all the three neighbourhoods, Hrasnica, Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, Muslims keep the Serbs as hostages?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely true. I have found an original - not a photocopy, but an original - bearing a blue stamp which clearly shows what it was that we wrote, and it's true that Muslims were hostages in Sokolovic Kolonija. In December, they sent us a list of those intended for an exchange, including women and children, and some killed individuals. I think the total was 266 of those who were intended to be exchanged --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you right that the Muslims held 266 Serbs as hostages, and that the women they held were pregnant?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In December of 1992, the Exchange Commission from the municipality of Ilidza sent to me, and the MUP at Ilidza, a list of some 266 individuals who would be allowed to leave. They were minors, children, pregnant women. And the list also included individuals who had long been killed; for instance, Zdravko Gligorevic is one for whom I knew that this was a fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So to avoid any confusion, it was the Muslims holding the Serbs hostages?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, it makes mention of break-ins into apartments, names mentioned, and here you appeal to the European Community to immediately set up a mixed commission which would --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, tour each flat and go in a fact-finding mission as to the situation with regards to the Serbian population in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was such a commission established?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last thing we will deal with before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In relation to this event we just discussed, Mr. Prstojevic, was the Ilidza municipality authority under pressure from those who were kept, tortured, et cetera, and were you asked to explain to them what were the reasons why you couldn't help them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had a hundred problems, and this was one of them. On the 22nd of April, an APC, which set out for an exchange of Serb TO members and Muslims, had skidded off the road. The crew, all of whom were people from Ilidza, were taken prisoner. Let me mention just one name, Stevan Djokanovic. These prisoners would be killed, in early May, somewhere, apparently, near to the police hall. Their relatives approached us and appealed to us for assistance, but we were helpless there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me be quite precise. The JNA sent an APC to separate the Serbs from the Muslims. The Muslims captured them and killed them in this large parkland near to the police hall?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Caterpillar track on the APC that fell off, and that's how they captured them. But they couldn't reason with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the last thing I'm going to ask you is this: Were there any problems, and was it difficult to prevent people from taking revenge on the Muslims living in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information to the effects that the Serbs in Ilidza would engage in any sort of revenge. We were not of that sort of character that we would engage in revenge. It was more the refugees from Central Bosnia and elsewhere who had that sort of nature. Certain problems arose from this situation. We had a Serb from Central Bosnia killing another Serb because he wanted to take his cow to feed the army, and he killed him because he needed the cow to feed his family. It was a Bugarin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Bugarin is the surname, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his first name is Dragan. Dragan Bugarin. He was a scoundrel. He wanted to take the cow from this other Serb for his own troops, and the other man killed him because he had to feed his family.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are we going to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we call up 65 ter 01510.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I will try, in the briefest of the terms, to present to you the substance of a number of documents, and it will be up to you to confirm them or deny them. This is a bulletin of daily events, issued by the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was called at that point. And the first paragraph says that during the past night, between the 3rd and the 4th of May, an attack was launched on the Serbian territory, on JNA facilities, by paramilitary forces of former Bosnia-Herzegovina; that Ilidza came under attack from the direction of airport. Is this what the document says?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was: Does the document correspond with the events as they transpired between the 3rd and the 4th of May of that year?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that a Muslim TO vehicle was passing through the area, and whoever refuses to respond to their calls is being mistreated, their house damaged, et cetera. Was this true?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't informed of this particular incident, but I know that at that point in time, there were less than 100 Serbs in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Prstojevic, that we had never forced the Muslims and Croats to join our army?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but there is information in the Muslim documents as to how many Serbs were present in their army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph says that they came to learn that a new Muslim-Croatian MUP station was set up in Stup, and it says that Edin Mlivic was the chief who, before the outbreak of hostilities, was chief at Ilidza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Around the 6th of April, 1992, the Muslims would set up the War Presidency of the municipality of Ilidza, and they would station their MUP in this particular neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It just may be time for another reminder for the witness to attempt to place a pause between the question and answer. On a number of occasions recently, his answer began as the translation was still being rendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's very difficult for us to follow, Mr. Prstojevic. Please put a pause. Yes, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they set up their own Muslim municipality of Ilidza on the 6th of April, in accordance with the prewar negotiations, or was this something else?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, they set up their own municipality, but they also set up a war presidency which included even a Serb, Dusan Sehovac, for instance. And I know that they chose, as the seat of the Muslim MUP of that Muslim municipality, Stup I, and I have reliable evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit the document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 01512.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a daily report issued by the Ministry of the Interior for the 8th of May. The fourth bullet reads: "The Serbian forces continue to hold a firm grip on all the territories seized in all the areas of the town. In particular, control was established over the parts of the town running along the valley of the River Miljacka ..." Et cetera: "The Serb forces are in full control, and in some areas life of all the inhabitants in the area has returned to normal." Does this correspond to the situation as it was ahead of that large attack on the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because as of the 22nd of April, we didn't have those frontal attacks and life could return to normal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 65 ter 30750.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telephone conversation, or rather its transcript, between you and a man called Grandic on the 12th of May. And on page 1, we can see that you are asking to speak to someone who's in charge. Can we have the next page in Serbian and keep the English. You got hold of someone who introduces himself to you as Lieutenant-Colonel Grandic. You say: "Grandic," which means you're not really familiar with him -- Could we have the next page in English, please. You are seeking to speak to Colonel Gagovic, and you want him to do something to allow you to defend yourselves from those -- from the lot from Hadzic. Does it mean that on this date, the Muslims from Hadzici were attempting a breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. On the 12th, the Muslims would launch a great offensive at the Serb-held positions in Hadzici and at the Local Commune of Blazuj, at the Mostarski intersection. Obrad Popovic, the TO staff commander, and I would be compelled to deploy elements of our forces from the eastern side from Vojkovici and Kasindol to western side of the municipality on that particular day. In this way, we would practically leave them in the hands of the TO Hadzici. And at twilight, they would be handed over to their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This man, Grandic, informs you here that he survived the column. Is it the column of the 3rd of May, when the Command of the 2nd Military District was being evacuated and came under attack by groups of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it refers to, and that was unheard of. Let me remind you that in 1912, when the Serbian Army liberated Skadar, it had against itself the Turkish Army, but they allowed them to withdraw towards Istanbul in a dignified way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, you go on to explain that this was a struggle for survival, that Hadzici was as shaky as a castle made of cards, et cetera. Is this not yet another proof of the fact that you were unable to convince the JNA into defending you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fully correct. The JNA did not participate in the fighting at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3075, please. 1D3075.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is Ranko Mandic, the person in charge of the Information Service of the Crisis Staff, who cautions about the falsity of all the agreements. And he says in paragraph 2, just as the agreement that was reached unanimously and made public by the BiH Presidency, the Muslim forces opened fire from all of their assets at Ilidza and Hadzici, their goal being to seize the area of Hadzici, et cetera: "At Sokolovic Kolonija, a settlement situated near Ilidza, they are even seizing bacon and lard from the Serbian population, and they do not allow the Serbs from Hrasnica, Sokolovic and Butmir to leave these neighbourhoods, even though they have signed agreements to the contrary." Is that consistent with the events of the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 30751.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your telephone conversation of the 13th of May, of the same day, therefore, where you managed to get hold of Colonel Gagovic at last. I do believe that there's a translation of this. Could we have the next page in Serbian and in English, I believe. There must be a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that there's not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Then I'll just have to read a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here: "Those down there are constantly in contact with me." And you were asked: "Which ones?" And then you say: "Those on the boundary with Hadzici." And then the person you are talking to says: "Well, I believe ..." And then you say: "Well, I'll have to return fire." And then the other individual tells you: "You do know -- don't -- you do know that --" I'm having problem with time. So you were asked who was it who was engaging in contact with you, and then you say: "Those on the boundaries with Hadzici." And then you say: "I'll have to return fire." And the unidentified male says: "You do know -- don't -- you do know that -- it's been denied. I think that the Serbian Assembly agreed that the truce, as it were, just as did the army and the other ones, that focus should 100 per cent be on the negotiations in the next couple of days, so let's leave it at that, please." And then further down, the individual is asking you: "Are they opening fire?" And you say: "Yes, they are." And you also say: "And they are building up forces." And the unidentified male says: "Well, if they are opening fire, everything that is done in defence is allowable, but one should exercise full restraint ..." Et cetera. Is this a conversation with the Lukavica Barracks, where this member of the Yugoslav People's Army is trying to dissuade you from engaging in a fight, reminding you of the truce announced by the Serbian Assembly, and in response you say that the municipality may fall unless you return fire?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything you've said is absolutely correct and is consistent with the developments at the time at the front-lines of the municipality of Hadzici and the edges of the Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we'll admit this. 1212, Exhibit D1212.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the problem is, Your Honour, there's no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was mistaken. We'll mark it for identification, pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 30761.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What follows next is your feverish activity on the 14th of May, 1992. Do you recall that date, Mr. Prstojevic? Just yes or no. Let's keep it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's only a day after the other thing. Yesterday, it was the 13th; today, it is the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your conversation with a certain Tadija. Maybe it's Tadija Manojlovic, who later became the commander of the Artillery of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. And I may be mistaken, on the other hand. Further down, you say: "I am expecting combat to break out any moment here on the right flank near Vrutaci." And further down, you say: "It is almost started." Can we have the next page in Serbian, please. This is what you say here: "Please, as soon as you have the time, come in. I need people urgently to come back to the positions. I'm expecting fire or fighting to break out any moment." Can we have the next page, please. And then he says: "All right, I'll tell them, him, so let him --" And then you say: "Tell Gagovic." Is this fresh evidence that the JNA is totally unfeeling in respect of what you are suffering on the 13th of May, and they are just not moving?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that on that day, at 5.08, we were attacked at the front-line, and the front-line was over 20 kilometres' long. We had eight fatalities and fifty wounded, and the fighting went on for twelve hours, more than that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3076, please. We are going to get the English version too, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your people from the Information Service, Ranko Mandic, Nedeljko Zukic, that are issuing this piece of information, and it says: "It is now 1730 hours and the battles at Ilidza go on. They started at 5.08, and they've been going on for more than 12 hours." And then also: "We found out that while withdrawing from Otes, the enemy intentionally fired at a residential building with gas installations in order to destroy this Croat neighbourhood which had refused to fight on the side of the Muslims." Does this correspond to what happened until 5.30?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is fully correct, and there are Croatian sources that say the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not evident, on the basis of this, that it is one neighbourhood fighting against another neighbourhood, and that there are no foreign troops there, or, rather, troops from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite clear that there are no troops from anywhere else. Any well-intentioned person sees that. However, I have to point out that on this day of the fighting, about 10 of Arkan's men were participating in this as well. Perhaps there were a few more. They are involved in the Stup front-line, where the fighting actually started.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1214, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 30754.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yet another one of your many telephone conversations on that day. You are talking to Djogo, so this is Djogo and Prstojevic, and then Prstojevic and Radivoje Grkovic. It says here -- or, rather, Djogovic [phoen] is informing you that he has talked to Gagovic and that contact should be established with Deda and Sjever. And then you say there is an all-out attack in your area. And then he says: "All right, it's the same over here too." Is he talking about the eastern part of Ilidza, east of the airport, Nedzarici? Where are they at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, they are in Nedzarici; that is, Captain Djogo. However, the attack at the airport is an attack at the airport area, Ajramsko Naselje [phoen]. It is a single whole. There was a strong attack against the airport on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The JNA is not getting involved, they are only talking; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they are in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 30758.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the same day. It is Djogo and Mandic -- and Mandric who is talking. It's probably Mandric. Mandric says: "Here we are. We've taken Cenex and we're holding it." So there was a counter-offensive and Cenex was taken. Does Cenex belong to the minister of the interior, Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that it was his building that was under construction during the war, enormous concrete hallways and elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look further down. Mandric says: "There is an assault from another side through a street." And then it says: "From Energoinvest?" And Mandric is saying: "Can you send me an APC, by any chance?" Can we have the Serbian version, page 2. Djogo says: "No way. You know how heavy the attacks are from Vojnicko Polje, I think, Alipasino. These men here have just called Gagovic. Now, we have to hold on to this at any cost." And then he says: "I have information that 500 had set out from Alipasino, 200 from Vojnicko." And then he's talking about that assault in that street, is this street-fighting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an urban area. It is street-fighting. Throughout the war, we were able to go to Nedzarici only during the night, but we did hold that settlement: As for this assault from Vojnicko Polje that is referred to, that is close to the airport and Ajramsko Naselje. If you look at it from their side, it is the left flank, and the right faces Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are being quoted here as having said that: "Stup has to be cleared today." Cleared of what, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have defended ourselves, and now I am putting forth a clear request that it has to be clear of enemy soldiers or that enemy soldiers should be mopped up. At one point, our troops want to withdraw. And this is what I'm literally saying to Captain Djogo, Tell them it's better to get killed by the Turks than to get killed by the Serbs, because we are resolute, we do not have any reserve positions. It is only possible to enter Serb neighbourhoods by going over the dead, going over dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? The transcript doesn't reflect that you said that -- you said that that there were no reserve positions, that there can be no withdrawal. That's what you meant; right.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Throughout the war, Ilidza did not have any reserve positions, throughout the war, during those four years of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if the front-line breaks, everything is done and over with?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it breaks, then they withdraw to the next house, and then they try to retake what was lost. And there are examples like that. Murat Kahrovic describes this in detail in his book, "How We Defended Sarajevo: The 1st Sandzak Brigade." From July until the end of December, they all got killed in this part of the front-line here, and he describes all of that very specifically and in detail.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, or, rather, marked for identification, because Mr. Prstojevic is not one of the interlocutors, but people who he does know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1216, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I just want to make a request that the accused not depart from the text of the documents in question, imposing questions. I mean, there are many formulations posed to the witness with which he's asked to agree, but, in any event, they shouldn't take the form of -- and particularly, for the record, of appearing to be part of the document in question. In this case, it was an addition to what was ostensibly said by one of the participants in the intercept after it was clear that there was no further comment in the transcript from that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Excellency. I just wish to give you the entire name. For example, if it is put in very brief terms, "Vojnicko," it is actually "Vojnicko Polje," so that's why I'm trying to clarify matters. 30757, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I notice Mr. Karadzic did that as well. I didn't object to that. It was the last comment after the interlocutor Djogo had finished speaking, and there was an additional that was attributed to him after there was no further comment from Djogo other than: "Okay."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to confirm whether this was a conversation between you and Mr. Gagovic on that same day? So you finally managed to get in touch with him and you're flattering him a bit, Great leader, whatever. And you say: "I do not have power for recoilless guns." And he says: "I know all about that." And you say: "Can anyone bring it to me? And four of their APCs are in the middle of a combat by the Institute." Gagovic says: "Okay." And then you say: "I know you want to help. Do this and we can shake on it when I come to see you tomorrow." "Okay." So you promised that you would kiss him, embrace him only if he helped you? Was this your conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I listened to this conversation and I recognised my own voice, but I know that on that very difficult day during the war, I had this conversation at this institute. Quite a few of our men got killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1086, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is that conversation during which you are leaving your rifle aside. It's the end of the day. And as you had put it, if it is looked at as an isolated thing, you like a raven, everything is so dark. Do you say: "Good evening"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this, at any rate, after 5.00, which means that the fighting had gone on for over 12 hours? If it started at 5.08, and it is a May evening, so it's rather late, is it correct that the fighting went on considerably longer than 12 hours?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at different front-lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The men who got killed and who were wounded, were they persons who had lived there, and are their families there, the families that are supposed to bury them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. These are all local people from Ilidza, from different neighbourhoods that are the closest to the defence line. We mobilised people in such a way so that they would be defending their own homes, where it was the quickest for them to reach the front-line on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that moment, are you the number-one man, with top responsibility, as far as these people are concerned?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. If anything is wrong, then I'm to be blamed the most. And if things go well, then it is everyone's merit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Because of this tremendous psychological pressure and the very real armed pressure, did some people -- some Serb officials resign even before this happened because they could not take all that responsibility?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some officials tender their resignations, and some just ran away, fled from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is identified here is that Mika called you: "Mika called me." And you are trying to establish what it was that Mika wanted, and they are informing you that they have people from Kotorac. And you are asking whether they were arrested, and what they did with them, and so on and so forth. You see this entire conversation, and he says: "They're down there by the road. Women and men are separated." And then it says: "I've just been informed men are in prison in Kula and the women have gone towards Butmir." Can we have the next page in Serbian. I think that we have the correct page in English. And now here you inquire whether they were mopping up Kotorac. And further on, we can all see the conversation, and you are asking him -- appealing to him: "In God's name," you say, "why did you take women to Butmir?" And he says: "Not to the KP Dom, but to Butmir, the settlement, so to speak." I'm just paraphrasing it now. I'm not reading. And you said, They couldn't go to Butmir because we would be mopping up Butmir in time as well, and so on and so forth. And down towards the bottom: "Come on, tell me. The one who would accept the Orthodox faith might stay, and so also the women and the children." Do you remember what they published in the "Vox" magazine, that the Serbs who would convert to the forefathers' faith of Islam would be safe?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look here, Mr. President. At this moment, I didn't know what my name was. I had eight killed, fifty wounded, and my territory was in danger. Someone called me here and used his code-name, which we didn't normally do, and someone was interfering with the conversation. And later on, I called the man who was the manager of the chicken farm, but I was so beside myself, I was probably talking with Milenko Tepavcevic, who was the chief of the Public Security Station in Kula. I say "probably." And I asked to speak to him. I'm not aware that I'm already speaking with him, but everything seems to indicate that I am. And practically what is requested here is that I should give my approval. It is well known when darkness falls in the month of May. So for what had happened up until 2.30 p.m., what's the substance? On that day, from the enclave of Gornji Kotorac, which is two kilometres in the depth of our territory, they joined the general all-out attack on Ilidza, but to the east. There was a reaction to that from the police station in Kula, which had numerous staff and which is at the bottom of the hill in the direction to this settlement. It is actually a part of the settlement. And the people from the military police, or the Territorial Defence, or the JNA; I could not determine which of these. But it says here it was Grujo Kutlaca, literally, was wearing a camouflage uniform, and the Territorial Defence at that moment did not have camouflage uniforms; but it's all the same, who it was. The essence is this: They launched an attack against Kasindol and lower settlement of Lubore [phoen] and in the direction of Donji Kotorac. The MUP reacted, and the police frisked and seized weapons. It's noted how many weapons they took away. Some Muslims remained there, but it was more or less just 70 households. The others, according to their own wish, went wherever they wanted to in luxury cars, on tractors. And between the place where I was talking and the Muslim defence line, the distance was only 300 metres in one place. In another place, it was 700 metres. So the population had decided that who wanted to stay could stay, and who wanted to leave could leave, according to their wish. The able-bodied were taken to prison if they were found with weapons, and they remained in prisons for about 10 days and then they were set free. So all the discussion about the 70 households is here, if someone wants to try to use this as a basis to build a theory that we were doing anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you ever -- did it ever come to pass that Butmir would also be mopped up, or was Butmir left in peace from our part?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left Butmir in peace. And, look here, I was not doing anything. Butmir would be mopped up, so Sokolovic Kolonija would be mopped up, Hrasnica would be mopped up. But when I calm down for a minute or two, I then said, Butmir will be mopped up. Go on and tell the men. It was just formal. It was moral. We never attacked these areas. In order to attack them, we had to have an order from the corps, an order from brigades, and no one could have that. I claim this with full responsibility, and no one had it. There is also a point from the meeting which took place, I believe, on the 12th or the 20th of September, when General Mladic said, Liberate. That was a strategic trick, because during passing on the information and reporting that would reach the soldiers at the lowest level and the soldiers' wives, and therefore the Muslims would learn it too, that was just a trick so that later on Lukavac 93 operation would be launched. I considered this later on, and it was 90 per cent like this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It was not recorded that the witness said at one moment, I became very angry, but then he added he calmed down very quickly. Tomorrow, or, rather, on Monday, we will show a map of Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that from Butmir, they attacked only the airport, and that the Serbian settlement of Ilidza was not attacked by the local Muslims, and that that was why you did not turn against Butmir?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one or two first battles, they attacked Ilidza, and they would have two APCs from there. But on the 14th, when I talk about this battle, of the 180 of their soldiers, 140 deserted immediately after the first clash and, I don't know, several hours of fighting. And later on, as it developed, after this 14th of May, and on the 4th of August, during the attack on the eastern part, they simply will not have enough strength or will to attack us, because they had casualties on the side and the local Muslims did not wish to lose their lives and to attack. And we did not touch them later on. It was practically decent peace that we had, especially towards the centre of Ilidza. And in the eastern area, in the direction of Kotorac, well, there, those from Donji Kotorac killed some civilians by sniper fire, civilians and passersby on the Lukavica-Bijelo Polje-Kupres-Trnovo road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is a document that has already been admitted. Can we now have 1D3077, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Prstojevic, that whether one becomes angry or not, flares up or not, it does not really mean that if you said something, that it was really implemented? Would you agree with me that much more is said than done?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I simply lost control over myself, and nothing came about of what I then said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the police station in Ilidza, the National Security Department, and it says here: "Attack on Ilidza, the 14th of May." And it says: "Retain this analysis --" or, rather: "Keep it." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correctly described here, how things developed, and the last three lines: "At 0550 hours, an infantry attack which was fierce started with fire opened from infantry weapons on the vital sections of Ilidza," as it says? And up there, it says on the 13th of May, at 1700 hours, it was called to the police station that an attack against Ilidza was to be launched from the direction of Stupsko Brdo? Did your police station inform you about this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, this is the original report from the Serbian National Security. And if you can see, our press centre also announced the attack one day ahead. So everything you can see here is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please see page 5. Another page onwards, please. And in English -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that: "During the attack on Ilidza, the following members of the Serbian forces were killed: Andzic, Sava; Gajic, Zoran; Janjic, Dragisa; Kocic, Andras." And you also seem to have had a Hungarian living in Ilidza; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that, but I can judge by his last name. Of these men who were killed, I only know one, for instance. I knew one at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And two other unidentified soldiers, you say a total of eight wounded and fifty -- or eight dead and fifty wounded?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know the wounded, more or less?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were all the locals. Generally, I recognise their last names. As soon as I see a last name, "Staka," for example, he's from the Vrelo Bosne. Then Suco Naselje, Nedzarici, Vojnicko Polje, Pindzo, directly at the front, where most people were killed, that's where their houses were. Krajisnik, directly at the front-line. Tosic, likewise. These were the men who were closest to the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see the last page, please, so that we could see the number of the 50 wounded, so that we wouldn't owe anything to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kocic is the last name. The first name was not known at the moment. Is that the list of the 50 men?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, but the best information can be obtained from our Zica Hospital. But this is correct, because it was made after the battle.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you agree, Mr. Prstojevic, on Monday, we would discuss the alleged ethnic cleansing, and para-groups and paramilitaries, and then I would like us to shed light, in the time that remains, on the nature of our relations between you and me. So if we could now have 65 ter 30549. In one of your statements, you confirmed that before the war or, at any rate, before the multi-party political system was introduced, we had not known each other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's absolutely correct. It wasn't only you; I didn't know anyone from the leadership of Republika Srpska and the SDS before the war. At the Municipal Board of the SDS in Ilidza, I only knew one man from Kasindol. We were completely unknown to one another. We didn't know what the other person used to do before the war, what education he had, how worthy or unworthy he was, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that because not only the government changed, but so did the whole system, Mr. Prstojevic, and the new authorities included people who previously did not have any power?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, because they now entered the politics, they became members of political parties. These were people who had not been in power earlier, and, therefore, their names were not well known.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at the next page. I believe we need the next page in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just focus on this part. It's the fourth or fifth from above in Serbian, "Nedjeljko Prstojevic": "This is not the line, you say. We honour what you said when you did as you say. Any man of another ethnicity who is in favour of Yugoslavia has a maximum of -- so the line would not be according to membership, he's not even a member. Simply, he is not good enough. Then we should leave these men, the Council of the Assembly ..." And so on. You are talking about relieving someone, relieving a person from his or her post, and this is what we're discussing. And you confirm that you know that my position is that ethnicity cannot be an important factor; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this person was the secretary of the Kasindol Local Commune, and it was a Serb woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, I tell you: "Okay, listen. Let me tell you, let -- first, set up the commission, have a commission be set up, and someone from our Executive Board should be in it to see whether the allegations are correct ..." And so on: "This has to be systematised and well documented. Otherwise, it will cause divisions of the Serbian people and will cause breaks among the Serbian people to appear. In some cases, it is better and wiser not to do it. That is not the most urgent job at this moment." Could we see the next page, please, in both versions.
